title: Richard II
author: William Shakespeare
setting: England and Wales, 1398 to 1400, from the lists at Coventry to a cell at Pomfret
lengthNote: Around 2,800 lines, and not one of them in prose
openingLine: Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster, Hast thou, according to thy oath and band, Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son?
summary: A king who believes the crown was fixed on him by God seizes his cousin's inheritance to pay for a war in Ireland, and finds that the cousin comes home for the land and stays for the throne. Bolingbroke wins without a battle; Richard loses without a defeat. The play is written entirely in verse, so the man who cannot hold a kingdom can still out-speak everyone in it, and the deposition turns into an argument about what words a king is made of.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Richard II
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions vary by a line or two, and quarto and Folio witnesses differ over the deposition passage in 4.1.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Early enough that the two parts of Henry IV and Henry V are still ahead of it.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise; the deposition material was advertised as an addition only in 1608.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare keeps the chronicle sequence and invents the interior life that goes with it.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act IV is a single scene, and it is the longest and most dangerous in the play.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The quarrel, and the banishments
structure.summary: Bolingbroke accuses Mowbray of treason and of Gloucester's murder, a charge that leads back towards Richard himself. Richard first orders trial by combat and then stops it mid-ceremony, banishing both men. The interruption saves him from a verdict and costs him the only two men who could have given one.

scenes.title: The accusation
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke and Mowbray throw down their gages before the king, who fails to reconcile them.

scenes.title: Gloucester's widow
scenes.summary: The Duchess asks Gaunt for revenge; he answers that the quarrel is God's, because the king ordered the murder.

scenes.title: The lists at Coventry
scenes.summary: Richard halts the combat at the trumpet and banishes Mowbray for life and Bolingbroke for ten years, then six.

scenes.title: Farming the realm
scenes.summary: Alone with his favourites, Richard mocks Bolingbroke's popularity and decides to lease out England to fund the Irish wars.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: An inheritance seized, and an army landed
structure.summary: Gaunt dies telling Richard that a king who rents out his country is a landlord. Richard confiscates the Lancastrian estate on the spot, which converts a private grievance into a constitutional one: he has broken the law of inheritance that his own title rests on. Before he reaches Ireland, Bolingbroke has landed at Ravenspurgh.

scenes.title: Ely House
scenes.summary: Gaunt's dying speech on England; Richard seizes his lands, and York warns him what that means.

scenes.title: The Queen's foreboding
scenes.summary: The Queen feels a grief with no cause yet; news arrives that Bolingbroke has landed with a growing following.

scenes.title: Gloucestershire
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke gathers support and tells York he has come only for his own inheritance.

scenes.title: The Welsh camp disperses
scenes.summary: Salisbury watches the Welsh troops leave on a rumour that the king is dead.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Richard’s return, and Flint Castle
structure.summary: Richard lands from Ireland, greets the soil of his kingdom, and then loses the country in three scenes of bad news. At Flint Castle he comes down from the walls to meet Bolingbroke in the base court, a piece of staging that settles the question before either man says what he wants. In the garden scene the collapse becomes an argument about husbandry.

scenes.title: Bristol
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke sends Bushy and Green to execution, itemising their offences first.

scenes.title: The coast of Wales
scenes.summary: Richard argues that no sea can wash the balm from a king, and then hears the reports that knock the claim down.

scenes.title: Flint Castle
scenes.summary: Northumberland delivers Bolingbroke's terms; Richard comes down to the base court and is taken to London.

scenes.title: The garden
scenes.summary: A gardener and his man read the state of England off a neglected garden, and the Queen overhears the news of the deposition.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The deposition in Westminster Hall
structure.summary: One scene, and the whole political argument is inside it. Carlisle predicts civil war if a subject crowns himself, and is arrested for saying so. Richard is made to hand over the crown in public, and makes the ceremony into a performance of his own fall, calling for a mirror and breaking it.

scenes.title: The deposition
scenes.summary: Gages fly over Gloucester's death, Carlisle prophesies, Richard resigns the crown and smashes the glass.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Richard’s imprisonment and murder
structure.summary: Richard is parted from the Queen and sent north. York uncovers his own son in a plot and denounces him, which shows what loyalty now costs a family. In prison Richard thinks his way through the only kingdom he has left, and Exton kills him on the strength of a question Bolingbroke asked aloud and never answered.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: Richard and the Queen say goodbye on the way to the Tower; she is sent to France.

scenes.title: Aumerle's plot
scenes.summary: York finds a treasonous bond on his son and rides to betray him to the new king.

scenes.title: The pardon
scenes.summary: Father and mother plead on opposite sides; Henry pardons Aumerle and hunts the rest.

scenes.title: Exton hears a wish
scenes.summary: Exton repeats the king's question about a living fear and decides it was an order.

scenes.title: Pomfret
scenes.summary: Richard compares his cell to the world, hears music out of time, and is killed.

scenes.title: Windsor
scenes.summary: Henry receives the rebels' heads and then Richard's coffin, banishes Exton and vows a crusade.

characters.name: King Richard II
characters.role: King of England, grandson of Edward III
characters.summary: He begins as a king who thinks the title does the work for him, and becomes, once it is taken away, the best speaker in the play. Everything he loses politically he recovers as language, which is why an audience that would not follow him into battle follows him into prison.
characters.clue: He calls for a looking-glass in the middle of losing a kingdom, and dashes it on the floor when the face in it is still his own.

relationships.label: cousin, rival and prisoner of
relationships.note: They are grandsons of the same king, which is the whole difficulty.

characters.name: Henry Bolingbroke
characters.role: Duke of Hereford, later King Henry IV
characters.summary: He says very little about what he wants and gets all of it. The play never gives him a soliloquy, so an audience must judge him by timing alone: he lands to claim an inheritance, accepts a crown he never demands, and ends by disowning the murder he asked for out loud.
characters.clue: He comes home for his father's land, says nothing about the throne, and is king within two acts.

characters.name: John of Gaunt
characters.summary: He refuses to avenge his brother's murder because the king ordered it, and then spends his last scene saying everything he has held back. His speech on England is a complaint about leases and parchment bonds, not a patriotic anthem, and the play takes his estate away before his body is cold.
characters.clue: Dying, he puns on his own name, calls the king a landlord, and says England has conquered itself.

characters.name: Duke of York
characters.role: Edmund of Langley, Richard's uncle and Lord Governor of England
characters.summary: Left to hold the kingdom with no troops and no instructions, he changes sides slowly and in public, which makes him the play's honest measure of how fast legitimacy moves. By Act V he is denouncing his own son to prove a loyalty nobody asked him for.
characters.clue: He is told to defend a kingdom with an empty treasury, meets the invader on the road, and cannot decide whether to arrest him or dine with him.

characters.name: Thomas Mowbray
characters.summary: Accused of Gloucester's murder, he defends himself without ever explaining what happened, because the truth would implicate the king who is judging him. His farewell is about losing English, not England, and he dies offstage in Venice, the first of the play's exiles.
characters.clue: Banished for life, he grieves for his mother tongue and compares his own speech to a viol with the strings taken off.

characters.name: Earl of Northumberland
characters.summary: He does the work Bolingbroke will not be seen doing: carrying the demands to Flint, pressing Richard to read the list of crimes aloud, ordering him to the Tower. The Henry IV plays begin with the bill for his service arriving.
characters.clue: He never asks for the crown himself, but he is the man sent up to the castle wall to say what its terms will be.

characters.name: The Queen
characters.summary: Shakespeare ages a child bride into an adult woman so that the fall has a private witness. Her grief arrives before its cause does, and she is the only character who tells Richard to fight instead of talk, which he cannot do.
characters.clue: She feels a sorrow with no name in it before any messenger arrives, and later hears the worst news of her life from a gardener.

characters.name: Bishop of Carlisle
characters.summary: He makes the one speech in the play that names the consequence of what is happening, and is arrested before he finishes hearing the answer. His prophecy of English blood on English ground is also a trailer for the seven history plays Shakespeare had already written or would write.
characters.clue: He tells a hall full of lords that if they crown this man, the ground itself will be manured with English blood.

characters.name: The Gardener
characters.role: A servant in the Duke of York's garden
characters.summary: He has no name, one scene and the clearest political analysis in the play: a state is a plot of ground that needs pruning, and Richard has let the weeds take the light. He also knows about the deposition before the Queen does, which says something about how news travels.
characters.clue: He tells his man to bind up the apricocks, and makes a day’s weeding into a verdict on the reign.

themes.name: Divine right and the anointed body
themes.summary: Richard's whole defence is that kingship is a physical fact done to him with holy oil, not an office he holds on conditions. The play does not simply refute him: Bolingbroke wins, but the crown he takes never stops being described as stolen, and the next four plays pay for it.
themes.development: Asserted at full length in 3.2, tested against a landing army in 3.3, formally undone in 4.1, and mourned by the man who broke it in 5.6.

themes.name: Inheritance and the law of succession
themes.summary: Seizing Gaunt's estate is the hinge of the plot because Richard's own title comes from exactly the rule he breaks. York says so to his face: take away the right of an heir to succeed, and you have taken away the argument for being king. The play makes constitutional law a matter of personal cash flow.
themes.development: Richard leases the realm in 1.4, confiscates Lancaster in 2.1, and by 2.3 Bolingbroke is back claiming only what the law says is his.

themes.name: Words and names
themes.summary: Banishment is measured in breath, a name is a thing that can be taken off, and the deposition is conducted as a reading aloud. Richard discovers that a word from a king used to be an action and is now only a word, and he becomes a poet at the exact moment the sentence stops working.
themes.development: Bolingbroke counts four years cut from his exile in 1.3; Richard resigns his name in 4.1; at Pomfret in 5.5 he sets one biblical word against another and can settle nothing.

themes.name: England
themes.summary: The country is never an abstraction here. It is soil Richard greets by hand, a lease signed on rotten parchment, a sea-walled garden full of weeds, and a plot whose caterpillars Bolingbroke promises to pluck away. The metaphor lets servants pass judgement on kings without leaving their own subject.
themes.development: Gaunt's blessed plot in 2.1 is answered by the gardener's choked-up beds in 3.4, and by Carlisle's ground manured with English blood in 4.1.

themes.name: Time
themes.summary: Richard is repeatedly late: late to hear Gaunt, late back from Ireland, late to fight. In prison he works the image out in full, describing himself as a clock whose hands are his own fingers and whose chime is his groans, and concludes that the keeper of time has become time’s object.
themes.development: He wastes it in Acts I and II, hears music played out of time in 5.5, and admits the reversal in a single line before the keepers arrive.

themes.name: Ceremony and performance
themes.summary: Nearly every public event in the play is staged by someone: a trial by combat stopped at the trumpet, a descent from a castle wall, a resignation carried out with a crown held between two pairs of hands. Richard is the better performer and the worse politician, and the play does not say whether those are the same thing.
themes.development: Richard controls the ritual in 1.3, loses control of the staging at Flint in 3.3, and in 4.1 seizes the only role left by directing his own deposition.

techniques.name: Unbroken verse
techniques.definition: A play written entirely in metrical lines, with no prose scenes for servants, clowns or low life.
techniques.inThisBook: Gardeners, grooms and murderers all speak verse here, so there is no linguistic ground below the court to stand on and judge it from — the Henry IV plays open that ground immediately.

techniques.name: Extended conceit
techniques.definition: A single comparison developed at length until it has been pushed as far as it will go.
techniques.inThisBook: The crown as a well with two buckets and the prisoner as a clock are both worked out line by line, which is how Richard fills the time he can no longer command.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: A scene in which the surface action stands throughout for something else.
techniques.inThisBook: The garden in 3.4 is a working garden and a diagram of the realm, and the gardener never has to explain the second meaning.

techniques.name: Ritual inversion
techniques.definition: Taking the form of a ceremony and running it backwards.
techniques.inThisBook: The deposition in 4.1 uses the shape of a coronation — crown, sceptre, oath, anointing — with every element handed back instead of received.

techniques.name: Prophecy
techniques.definition: A speech that predicts consequences the audience can check against history.
techniques.inThisBook: Gaunt foretells Richard's burn-out and Carlisle foretells civil war; an Elizabethan audience knew the second prophecy had a hundred years of fulfilment behind it.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries the argument of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Gages thrown on the floor, a crown held between two men, and a mirror shattered in public do the work that a soliloquy would do elsewhere.

quotations.text: How long a time lies in one little word! Four lagging winters and four wanton springs End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Richard has just cut Bolingbroke's banishment from ten years to six.
quotations.analysis: Four years are measured in seasons, not numbers, so the mercy is felt as weather before it is understood as arithmetic. The couplet closes on ‘breath’, which makes royal authority a matter of moving air, a definition Bolingbroke will spend the play disproving by using armies instead.

quotations.text: The language I have learn'd these forty years, My native English, now I must forego: And now my tongue's use is to me no more Than an unstringed viol or a harp,
quotations.speaker: Mowbray
quotations.context: Sentenced to perpetual banishment, before he leaves for Italy.
quotations.analysis: Exile is described as a speech impediment, not a loss of land, which sets the play’s terms early: to be removed from England is to be removed from English. The instrument images are all of things still intact and simply unusable, and Richard will reach for the same idea when his own name is taken away.

quotations.text: Teach thy necessity to reason thus; There is no virtue like necessity.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Gaunt tries to console his banished son at the gate.
quotations.analysis: The advice is to argue backwards from what cannot be changed until it looks like a choice, and Bolingbroke refuses it outright in the lines that follow. It is worth noticing that Richard adopts precisely this habit of mind from Act III onwards, at which point Gaunt's consolation reads as a description of political defeat.

quotations.text: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired And thus expiring do foretell of him: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last, For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Dying at Ely House, waiting for the king to arrive.
quotations.analysis: 'Expiring' does double duty: it means dying and it means breathing out, so the prophecy and the last breath are the same event. Gaunt claims authority from his nearness to death, not from office, the only position from which anyone in this play tells Richard the truth to his face.

quotations.text: This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle, This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars, This other Eden, demi-paradise, This fortress built by Nature for herself Against infection and the hand of war,
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The opening of Gaunt's speech on England, still waiting for Richard.
quotations.analysis: The famous passage is a single sentence that does not reach its main verb for more than twenty lines, and when it arrives the verb is 'Is now leased out'. Quoted on its own the speech sounds like praise; read to the end of its grammar it is a complaint about a property transaction, and the delay is the point.

quotations.text: That England, that was wont to conquer others, Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The close of the England speech, moments before Richard enters.
quotations.analysis: The couplet turns a war verb inwards, so the country is both the army and the territory. It is also the play's structural thesis in two lines: nobody invades England here, and every wound in the next four acts is administered by an Englishman to another Englishman's title.

quotations.text: Landlord of England art thou now, not king: Thy state of law is bondslave to the law; And thou--
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The quarrel with Richard at the bedside, cut off by the king.
quotations.analysis: Gaunt swaps one title for another and the whole indictment is done. A landlord holds property for income; a king holds a country in trust, and the difference is the lease Richard has just signed. The dash marks the sentence Richard interrupts, and it is the last time anyone at court speaks to him like this.

quotations.text: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he; His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be. So much for that. Now for our Irish wars:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Richard's response to the news that Gaunt is dead.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of decorous condolence, then 'So much for that', and the tone drops from elegy to agenda inside a single verse line. The switch is the seizure of the Lancastrian estate happening at the level of style, several seconds before Richard says the word 'seize'.

quotations.text: The caterpillars of the commonwealth, Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Explaining to York, on the road in Gloucestershire, why he has come back armed.
quotations.analysis: Bolingbroke gives his invasion a horticultural justification: he is not raising an army, he is doing the weeding the owner has neglected. The gardener in 3.4 will use exactly this vocabulary without knowing it has already been used as a war aim, and the repetition is how the play checks Bolingbroke's claim against a disinterested witness.

quotations.text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; The breath of worldly men cannot depose The deputy elected by the Lord:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Newly landed from Ireland, before the bad news begins to arrive.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of chemistry, oil that water cannot lift, and within fifty lines it is answered by a series of reports, with no argument at all. Note that the sentence concedes more than it means to: if worldly breath cannot depose a king, the play then shows a king deposed by worldly hands instead.

quotations.text: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: After hearing that his Welsh army has dispersed and his favourites are dead.
quotations.analysis: Richard proposes the one activity no king can afford, which is sitting down, and he does it in the first person plural, recruiting the stage and the audience into an audience of his own. The list that follows is a catalogue of history-play plots, so in effect he is asking to be read, not obeyed.

quotations.text: All murder'd: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: The middle of the same speech on the coast of Wales.
quotations.analysis: The crown stops being an ornament and becomes a building with a tenant, and the tenant is a jester. ‘Hollow’ does two jobs, the shape of the metal and the emptiness of the office, and the word is still working in 4.1 when Richard hands the thing over and finds nothing inside it.

quotations.text: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Rebuking his followers for trying to comfort him.
quotations.analysis: ‘Subjected’ is the key word: it means made a subject and also made liable to, and Richard hears both meanings. Having spent a hundred lines insisting that a king is a different order of being, he now proves the opposite from the evidence of his own appetite.

quotations.text: What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be deposed? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name, let it go:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: On the walls at Flint Castle, after Northumberland brings Bolingbroke's demands.
quotations.analysis: Richard refers to himself in the third person throughout, as though reading the part of a king from a script someone else is writing. The questions are rhetorical but the answers are real concessions, so the speech gives away the kingdom in the grammar while the surface sounds like defiance.

quotations.text: Down, down I come; like glistering Phaethon, Wanting the manage of unruly jades. In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base, To come at traitors' calls and do them grace.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Descending from the castle wall to meet Bolingbroke in the lower courtyard.
quotations.analysis: Richard narrates his own stage movement, and a walk downstairs becomes the fall of a boy who could not hold his father’s horses. The pun on 'base' — the name of the yard, and a moral judgement — lets him lose the high ground physically while claiming it verbally, which is the whole tactic of his last three acts.

quotations.text: When our sea-walled garden, the whole land, Is full of weeds, her fairest flowers choked up, Her fruit-trees all upturned, her hedges ruin'd, Her knots disorder'd and her wholesome herbs Swarming with caterpillars?
quotations.speaker: A gardener's man
quotations.context: In the Duke of York's garden at Langley, while the Queen listens unseen.
quotations.analysis: A servant asks why he should tend one garden when the larger one is ruined, and in doing so repeats Gaunt's sea-wall and Bolingbroke's caterpillars from a position with nothing to gain. The play's political analysis is given to people with no rank at all, and delivered as a question about work.

quotations.text: And if you crown him, let me prophesy: The blood of English shall manure the ground, And future ages groan for this foul act; Peace shall go sleep with Turks and infidels,
quotations.speaker: Bishop of Carlisle
quotations.context: Interrupting the deposition in Westminster Hall; he is arrested for treason immediately afterwards.
quotations.analysis: ‘Manure’ is a farming word set in a cathedral register, and it carries the garden imagery into the political climax. The prophecy is unusual in Shakespeare for being entirely accurate and entirely useless: the audience already knows the Wars of the Roses happened, and the men on stage crown Bolingbroke anyway.

quotations.text: God save the king! Will no man say amen? Am I both priest and clerk? well then, amen.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Brought into Westminster Hall to surrender the crown in public.
quotations.analysis: He offers the loyal shout and then has to supply the response himself, playing both halves of a church service to an audience that will not join in. The line measures the deposition better than any argument in the scene: the form still exists, and nobody is willing to take part in it.

quotations.text: Now is this golden crown like a deep well That owes two buckets, filling one another, The emptier ever dancing in the air, The other down, unseen and full of water:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Holding one side of the crown while Bolingbroke holds the other.
quotations.analysis: Two men gripping a single object become a mechanism in which neither can rise without the other falling. The conceit also insults the winner: the bucket that goes up is the empty one, ‘dancing in the air’, while the full one sits unseen at the bottom.

quotations.text: Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be; Therefore no no, for I resign to thee. Now mark me, how I will undo myself;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Asked directly whether he is content to resign the crown.
quotations.analysis: The line will not settle into an answer: 'Ay' and 'I' sounded alike, so 'Ay, no' is also 'I, no', a man agreeing and cancelling himself in the same breath. It is the shortest statement in the play of what deposition does to a person whose identity was an office.

quotations.text: Was this the face that faced so many follies, And was at last out-faced by Bolingbroke? A brittle glory shineth in this face: As brittle as the glory is the face;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Looking into the mirror he has demanded, immediately before smashing it.
quotations.analysis: 'Face' is used as noun and verb within one line, so the word for a countenance becomes the word for bluffing, and the pun diagnoses his reign. Breaking the glass is meant to prove that grief has changed him; Bolingbroke's reply, that he has only destroyed the shadow of his face, is the coldest line in the play.

quotations.text: I have been studying how I may compare This prison where I live unto the world: And for because the world is populous And here is not a creature but myself, I cannot do it; yet I'll hammer it out.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Alone in the cell at Pomfret Castle.
quotations.analysis: This is the only soliloquy Richard has, and it opens by admitting that the comparison he wants to make does not work. 'Hammer it out' is a smith's phrase for beating metal into shape, so the thinking is presented as manual labour — the first honest work the play lets him do.

quotations.text: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me; For now hath time made me his numbering clock: My thoughts are minutes; and with sighs they jar Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Hearing music played badly in time, in the cell at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The chiasmus puts the same two words on either side of the verb and swaps who is doing what, which is the play's plot in nine syllables. What follows is mechanism, not self-pity: a man listing his own body as clockwork, down to the finger wiping tears off a dial.

quotations.text: 'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?' Was it not so?
quotations.speaker: Exton
quotations.context: Exton repeating to a servant what he heard the new king say.
quotations.analysis: The murder is commissioned by a question left hanging in a room, and the play stages the moment it is interpreted, not the moment it is ordered. Because Exton has to check the wording twice with a servant, Bolingbroke keeps the deniability that lets him banish the killer in the last scene.

quotations.text: I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land, To wash this blood off from my guilty hand:
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke, now King Henry IV
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, spoken over Richard's coffin.
quotations.analysis: The new reign opens with a promise of expiation that the two parts of Henry IV never allow him to keep; he is still planning the same crusade, and still failing to leave, in the play that follows. Washing also picks up Richard's claim that no water could remove the balm of kingship, and applies the image to a stain instead of a blessing.

timeline.label: Richard of Bordeaux is born
timeline.detail: Son of Edward the Black Prince, and grandson of Edward III.

timeline.label: Richard becomes king as a child
timeline.detail: He succeeds his grandfather Edward III at the age of ten, his own father having died the year before.

timeline.label: The Peasants' Revolt
timeline.detail: The young king faces the rebels in person, an episode Shakespeare leaves out of a play that begins seventeen years later.

timeline.label: Bolingbroke and Mowbray are banished
timeline.detail: The quarrel with which the play opens ends in exile, with no trial by combat.

timeline.label: Gaunt dies, Bolingbroke returns, Richard is deposed
timeline.detail: The confiscation of the Lancastrian inheritance and the landing at Ravenspurgh fall in the same year as the surrender of the crown.

timeline.label: Richard dies in captivity at Pontefract
timeline.detail: The play calls the castle Pomfret and gives him a murderer; the historical cause of death is not certain.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition gave Shakespeare the sequence of events for this play and the ones that follow it.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about this year, which places it at the head of the second sequence of English histories.

timeline.label: The first quarto is printed
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, without the deposition passage in 4.1.

timeline.label: A Richard II play is staged before the Essex rising
timeline.detail: Supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance of a play about Richard II on the eve of the revolt; the record does not name Shakespeare's text outright, but the subject was enough to make it dangerous.

timeline.label: Fourth Quarto adds the deposition scene
timeline.detail: The title page announces the Parliament scene and the deposing of King Richard as material now in print.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of a bad king who becomes a great poet
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats the play as the study of a temperament: a ruler whose gifts are entirely verbal and whose imagination only switches on once power is gone.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to leave Bolingbroke a blank, when the play’s silences around him look deliberate.

criticalViews.position: A play about the king's two bodies
criticalViews.summary: Legal and constitutional readings take Richard's insistence on anointing seriously, and follow what happens when the sacred person and the political office are pulled apart in public.
criticalViews.counter: Richard's own behaviour undermines the doctrine before Bolingbroke does: he breaks the law of inheritance that makes him king in the first place.

criticalViews.position: A play read for its politics in its own time
criticalViews.summary: The printing history and the performance on the eve of the Essex rising have long encouraged readings that treat the deposition as live and dangerous material for an Elizabethan audience.
criticalViews.counter: The evidence is thinner than the story suggests, and reading backwards from 1601 can flatten a play that spends most of its length on private grief.

essayQuestions.question: Is Richard deposed by Bolingbroke, or does he depose himself?
essayQuestions.focus: Agency, ceremony and the deposition scene
plan: Establish the legal position first: the seizure of Gaunt's estate in 2.1 breaks the inheritance rule that Richard's own title depends on, and York says so on stage.
Show Bolingbroke never stating a claim: track what he actually says in 2.3 and 3.3 against what his army achieves.
Read 3.3 as staging — the descent to the base court happens before any terms are agreed.
Take 4.1 slowly: Richard runs the ceremony, supplies the responses, calls for the mirror and narrates his own fall.
Conclude on 5.4, where the new king’s power works through a question, not a command, and ask which man is more responsible for the outcome.

essayQuestions.question: What does the garden scene contribute that the court scenes cannot?
plan: Set the scene in its place: 3.4 sits between the surrender at Flint and the deposition at Westminster, and nothing in the plot happens in it.
Trace the garden imagery backwards to Gaunt's sea-wall in 2.1 and Bolingbroke's caterpillars in 2.3.
Note that the gardener has no rank and no interest, which is what gives his judgement its authority.
Look at how the Queen, overhearing, changes political analysis into personal grief in the same scene.
Close on the fact that the servants speak verse: the play offers no comic underclass, so this is as far outside the court as it can reach.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play's language change once Richard stops being king?
essayQuestions.focus: Style, self-knowledge and the limits of eloquence
plan: Compare Richard's public style in Act I — royal plural, third person, crisp sentences of command — with his speech after 3.2.
Use the hollow crown speech to show the conceits lengthening as his options shorten.
Examine 4.1 for wordplay that works against him: 'face' as noun and verb, 'Ay, no' heard as 'I, no'.
Turn to 5.5 and the prison soliloquy, where he admits at the start that the comparison will not hold.
Judge whether the eloquence is compensation, self-deception, or the only form of understanding the play allows him.

essayQuestions.question: Does the play take sides between an incompetent king and a capable usurper?
plan: Set out Richard's record honestly: the murder of Gloucester behind the action, the farming of the realm in 1.4, the confiscation in 2.1.
Set out Bolingbroke's: no soliloquy, no stated claim, and a competence the play never denies.
Weigh Carlisle’s prophecy in 4.1, which is treasonous and, on the historical record, correct.
Consider Aumerle's plot in 5.2 and 5.3 as the first instalment of the disorder Carlisle predicted.
Finish on the last twenty lines, where the new king inherits a corpse, a guilt and a crusade he will never make.

discussionQuestions: Bolingbroke is given no soliloquy at all. Does that make him unreadable, or is the silence itself the characterisation?
Gaunt calls England a blessed plot and then says it has conquered itself. Which half of the speech does the rest of the play support?
Richard smashes the mirror to prove that sorrow has changed his face. What does it mean that the face is unchanged?
Why does Shakespeare give the clearest account of the kingdom's condition to a gardener with no name?
The play never lets anyone speak prose. What would be gained, and what lost, if the gardeners or the grooms did?
